title: Macro-Group Attack vs K=2 Evaluation on UNSW-NB15
hypothesis: K=1 underestimates because derived groups (state, is_sm, is_ftp) are causally coupled to proto/service, so macro-group K=1 would reveal additional vulnerability.
result: REFUTED — macro-group K=1 gives identical results to standard K=1 (96.0% = 96.0%)
actual_finding: K=2 vulnerability comes from CROSS-macro-group flips (service+state), not causal coupling within macro-groups.

k2_break_analysis.description: 4 samples that survived K=1 but broke at K=2:
k2_break_analysis.note: All involve CROSS-macro-group flips: service (Macro-B) + state (Macro-A)

group_flip_frequency_at_K2.note: is_sm_ips_ports and is_ftp_login never flipped at K=2 — derived groups are NOT the vulnerability drivers

conclusion.actual_mechanism: Model relies on multiple independent categorical features. K=1 perturbation of one group is insufficient; K=2 perturbation of two independent groups (e.g., service+state) collapses robustness.
conclusion.implication: The K=1 threat model is incomplete for UNSW-NB15 not because of causal coupling, but because it only explores 1 of 5 independent feature groups. The model is genuinely robust to single-feature attacks but vulnerable to multi-feature attacks.
conclusion.recommendation: For UNSW-NB15, report K=1 as a lower bound on vulnerability. K=2 evaluation (computationally expensive) reveals the true vulnerability.
